title: Form 1041 Explained: Filing Basics for Executors (October 2026)
summary: This October 2026 guide explains Form 1041 filing thresholds, deductions, schedules, and Schedule K-1 basics for executors.
body_markdown:
During estate settlement, income the estate earns after the person's death, such as interest, dividends, or rent, is reported on Form 1041, the federal income tax return for estates and trusts. Whether an estate must file depends on its gross income and whether any beneficiary is a nonresident alien. This guide explains key points for executors and families to be aware of, including: who must file, the filing threshold, what income and deductions are reported, Schedule K-1, and more.


**Key Takeaways**


- Form 1041 reports estate or trust income, separate from the deceased person's final Form 1040.
- Domestic estates file at $600 in gross income, or with any nonresident alien beneficiary, under the IRS filing requirements.
- Schedule K-1 reports each beneficiary's share of income, deductions, and credits.
- Elayne helps organize financial records for Form 1041 but does not prepare or file tax returns.


## What Is Form 1041?


Form 1041 is the U.S. Income Tax Return for Estates and Trusts.[An executor](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/information-for-executors) or trustee files it to report the estate’s or trust’s income, deductions, gains, losses, and income tax liability.


The deceased person’s final Form 1040, which determines[who receives tax refunds after death](https://www.elayne.com/resources/taxes-after-someone-dies-who-gets-the-tax-return-of-a-deceased-person) , reports personal income through death. Form 1041 reports estate income during administration, including income earned after death. An executor may need to file both returns.

## Who Must File Form 1041


Form 1041 filing requirements depend on the entity, as explained in[the IRS instructions on who must file](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i1041#id11) :


- Domestic decedent’s estates must file with gross income of $600 or more, or any nonresident alien beneficiary.
- Domestic trusts generally must file with any taxable income, gross income of $600 or more, or any nonresident alien beneficiary.
- Individual Chapter 7 or 11 bankruptcy estates have a separate filing threshold under the IRS bankruptcy estate filing requirements.Applicable tax year: years beginning in 2025.Filing threshold: gross income of $15,750 or more requires a return.


## The Filing Threshold for an Estate


The estate’s Form 1041 income threshold applies to gross income, not asset values. A house or bank balance alone does not trigger filing.


For example:


- An estate holding a home but receiving no post-death income may have no filing requirement.
- Example income: an estate receives $700 in post-death bank interest.Filing threshold: $600 in gross income under the IRS estate filing rules.Result: the estate must file.


Executors use income received during the estate’s tax year to assess this threshold, after[obtaining an EIN for the estate](https://www.elayne.com/resources/how-to-obtain-an-ein-for-an-estate) .


## Simple Trusts, Complex Trusts, and Grantor Trusts on Form 1041


Trust classification affects who pays income tax and how Form 1041 is prepared.


Trust type Income tax treatment


Simple Must distribute income annually; no principal distributions or charitable contributions. Beneficiaries generally report income.


Complex May retain income, distribute principal, or make charitable contributions. The trust generally pays tax on retained taxable income.


Grantor The owner generally reports income under special reporting rules.


Classification can change annually.


## What Income Gets Reported on Form 1041


Form 1041 reports estate or trust income, including:


- Interest and dividends received
- Income from rentals or businesses
- Capital gains from asset sales, not total proceeds
- Other taxable receipts, including certain retirement distributions governed by[inherited IRA distribution rules](https://www.elayne.com/resources/inherited-ira-distribution-rules)


For cash-basis taxpayers, income received before death generally goes on the final personal return. Income earned before death but received afterward generally goes on the recipient’s return.


The estate or a beneficiary may be that recipient; timing and recipient determine reporting.


## Deductions Available on Form 1041


Form 1041 deductions depend on the expense and applicable tax rules. Potential deductions include:


- Qualifying administration expenses, including attorney, executor, accounting, and court fees.
- Qualifying beneficiary distributions, capped by distributable net income (DNI), the tax calculation of income available to pass to beneficiaries.
- Qualifying charitable payments from gross income authorized by the governing document.
- Certain state and local taxes, subject to applicable limits.


Payment by the estate alone does not make an expense deductible.


## Form 1041 Schedules Explained


Schedule When it applies and what it calculates


D Reports capital gains and losses from asset sales or other capital transactions.


K-1 Reports each beneficiary’s allocated tax items.


G Calculates tax liability within Form 1041, including credits and other taxes.


I Calculates alternative minimum tax for estates or trusts.


J Calculates amounts for beneficiary tax treatment of certain complex trusts’ accumulation distributions.


The schedules needed depend on the estate’s or trust’s transactions and tax circumstances.


## Common Mistakes on Form 1041


Common Form 1041 errors involve separating income, calculating deductions, and reporting beneficiary distributions:


- Mixing the deceased person’s personal income with estate income, which can also complicate how to[notify the IRS of a death](https://www.elayne.com/resources/how-to-notify-the-irs-of-a-death-reporting-and-final-tax-responsibilities) .
- Skipping the calculation that determines whether filing is required.
- Sending required Schedules K-1 late or omitting beneficiaries.
- Overlooking adjustments when calculating distributable net income.
- Omitting an allowable income distribution deduction.
- Filing before[getting an EIN for an estate account](https://www.elayne.com/resources/how-to-get-ein-number-for-estate-account) .

## FAQ


### How do Elayne and a CPA support Form 1041 preparation if the estate sold a house?


A CPA experienced with estate income taxes can prepare the return and determine how the house sale is reported; Elayne helps organize records but does not prepare or file tax returns. The preparer generally needs the property’s date-of-death value, closing statement, and records of improvements and selling costs. Elayne’s shared dashboard can support the document handoff.


### What tax year does an estate use?


An estate’s first tax year begins on the date of death. The estate can use a calendar year or choose a fiscal year, which ends on the last day of any month within 12 months after the date of death. The choice is made on the estate’s first Form 1041. The[IRS accounting period rules](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i1041#en_US_2025_publink1000285987) cover these options.


### Does an estate need its own EIN to file Form 1041?


Yes. An estate is a separate taxpayer from the person who died, so Form 1041 uses the estate’s own employer identification number (EIN) instead of the deceased person’s Social Security number. The EIN is issued by the IRS and is requested on Form SS-4.


### Who signs Form 1041?


The fiduciary signs the return. A fiduciary is the executor, administrator, or trustee responsible for the estate or trust. When there are two or more fiduciaries, one authorized fiduciary is required to sign. A paid preparer who prepares the return for compensation also signs and provides identifying information on the form.


### When do beneficiaries receive a Schedule K-1?


The fiduciary provides each beneficiary with a copy of their Schedule K-1 by the due date of Form 1041, including any extension. The Schedule K-1 shows the beneficiary’s share of the estate’s income, deductions, and credits. Beneficiaries report those amounts on their own tax returns. The estate or trust generally claims an income distribution deduction for income passed out to beneficiaries.


### Is an inheritance taxable income to the beneficiary?


Property received as an inheritance is generally not treated as federal taxable income to the beneficiary. Income the estate earns and distributes is different. That income is reported to the beneficiary on Schedule K-1 and included on the beneficiary’s own return. Distributions from inherited retirement accounts follow separate rules, covered in this guide to[inherited IRA distribution rules](https://www.elayne.com/resources/inherited-ira-distribution-rules) . Some states also have their own inheritance or estate taxes, which are separate from Form 1041.


### Does an estate have to make estimated tax payments?


Estates and trusts generally make estimated tax payments, using Form 1041-ES, when they expect to owe tax. A decedent’s estate is exempt from estimated tax payments for tax years ending within 2 years after the date of death. After that period, the estimated tax rules apply in the same way as they do for other estates and trusts.


### What penalties apply to late filing or late payment?


The IRS charges a late-filing penalty of 5% of the unpaid tax for each month or part of a month the return is late, up to 25%. The late-payment penalty is 0.5% of the unpaid tax for each month or part of a month, up to 25%. Interest also accrues on unpaid tax. Penalties can be waived when the failure is due to reasonable cause. A separate penalty applies for failing to provide required information, such as Schedule K-1, on time.
